text: Fisk University is a private historically black liberal arts college located in Nashville, Tennessee, United States, founded in 1866. Its 40-acre (16 ha) campus, situated on a former Union Army base near downtown Nashville on Jefferson Street, was dedicated in 1876 and is now a National Historic Landmark. The campus was originally established as the Fisk Free Colored School on January 9, 1866, by John Ogden, Erastus Milo Cravath, and Edward Parmelee Smith of the American Missionary Association to educate freedmen during the Reconstruction era. The school was named after Clinton B. Fisk, a Union general and assistant commissioner of the Freedmen's Bureau, and secured a site in a former military barracks near Union Station, receiving $30,000 in government funds for its endowment. Enrollment quickly rose to 900, with students ranging in age from seven to 70. In 1867, the school was reorganized and incorporated as Fisk University to focus on higher education. James Dallas Burrus, John Houston Burrus, Virginia E. Walker, and America W. Robinson were the first students, with the two Burruses and Walker graduating in 1875, becoming the first African-American students to earn liberal arts degrees south of the Mason–Dixon line. The Tennessee Constitution of 1870 prohibited public schools from enrolling both Black and White students, prompting the University of Tennessee (then Eastern Tennessee University) to pay tuition for Black students through state scholarships from 1881 to 1883, a contract later changed to Knoxville College in 1884. In 1870, Adam K. Spence became principal and planned to expand the school to a larger campus in north Nashville, previously Fort Gillem. His wife, Catherine Mackie Spence, traveled across the U.S. to establish mission Sunday schools and raise funds through the American Missionary Association. Spence supported the founding of a student choir, which became the Fisk Jubilee Singers. In 1871, the choir toured the U.S. and Europe, singing before Ulysses S. Grant, Mark Twain, and Queen Victoria, popularizing spirituals like "Swing Low Sweet Chariot," and changing racial stereotypes. The tour raised nearly $50,000 (~$1.16 million in 2024), funding the construction of Jubilee Hall, the first building built for the education of freedmen in the South and now a National Historic Landmark. Cravath returned in 1875 and became the first president, overseeing curriculum expansion to include liberal arts, theology, and teacher training. James Griswold Merrill served as acting president from 1899 to 1901 and then as president until 1908. Fisk distinguished itself at the turn of the century by emphasizing liberal arts education, unlike many other Black colleges focused on vocational training. In 1910, it established a department of social science under George E. Haynes, becoming the first social work training center for African-American graduate students and a model for others. The school faced criticism for fostering an elitist reputation. From 1915 to 1925, Fayette Avery McKenzie served as president, developing Fisk into the premier all-Black college in the U.S., securing academic recognition from the Carnegie Foundation, Columbia University, and the University of Chicago, raising a $1 million endowment, and laying the foundation for accreditation—though he was forced to resign in 1924 and 1925 due to student protests over strict dress and extracurricular policies. Thomas Elsa Jones became president in 1925, seeking to diversify the faculty and build the school’s reputation. In 1930, Fisk became the first historically black institution to gain accreditation by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools and the first such institution approved by the Association of American Universities in 1933. Specialized program accreditations followed. In 1946, Charles S. Johnson became the sixth president and the first African-American president; a prominent sociologist and editor of Opportunity magazine, he expanded the Institute of Race Relations, established in 1942, which conducted research on racial disparities and helped develop desegregation strategies in schools, employment, and the military. In 1949, Fisk received the Stieglitz Collection of modern art from Georgia O'Keeffe, wife and executrix of Alfred Stieglitz, which includes 101 works by artists such as Cézanne, Renoir, Picasso, Rivera, Marsden Hartley, Arthur Dove, Charles Demuth, and O'Keeffe. In 1952, Fisk became the first predominantly Black college to earn a Phi Beta Kappa charter, with the Delta of Tennessee Chapter inducting its first members in April 1953. In 1960, Fisk students participated in the Nashville sit-ins, a key civil rights protest, and Martin Luther King Jr. spoke at the university in May 1960. Students John Lewis and Diane Nash led the protests, which led to Nashville becoming the first major Southern city to desegregate lunch counters, and both became early leaders of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). On April 8, 1967, a riot occurred near Fisk and Tennessee State University after Stokely Carmichael spoke at Vanderbilt University, viewed as a "race riot" with classist elements; protesters marched from Fisk to the Nashville courthouse to protest police brutality. In 1978, the Fisk University Historic District was added to the National Register of Historic Places. The campus underwent significant restoration in the 1990s with U.S. Congressional Grant assistance. From 2004 to 2013, Hazel O'Leary, former Secretary of Energy under President Bill Clinton, served as president and was the second woman to lead Fisk. On June 25, 2008, Fisk announced it had raised $4 million (~$5.7 million in 2024), ending nine years of budget deficits and qualifying for a Mellon Foundation challenge grant, though it still faced financial hardship and expressed possible closure. H. James Williams served as president from February 2013 to September 2015, succeeded by interim president Frank Sims, who was followed by Kevin Rome, appointed in March 2017 as the university’s seventeenth president. In June 2017, a memorial service for Ephraim Grizzard, an 1892 lynching victim, was held in the Fisk Memorial Chapel, and a plaque honoring Grizzard, his brother Henry, and Samuel Smith was installed at St. Anselm's Episcopal Church. In 2018, the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools placed Fisk on probation due to financial responsibility, research fund control, and federal/state compliance issues; the institution announced a fundraising record and increased enrollment the following year, and was removed from probation in 2020, maintaining accreditation. The Fisk University Historic District includes notable buildings such as Jubilee Hall, Little Theater, Harris Music Building, residential structures, and a limestone wall built around 1873. In the 1930s, the Olmsted Brothers designed the campus with a Beaux-Arts landscape. Fisk is home to a music literature collection founded by Carl Van Vechten, for whom the campus museum is named, and holds significant materials related to Charles W. Chestnutt. In 1930, Aaron Douglas was commissioned to paint murals for Cravath Hall, depicting the development of Black people in the Americas; the murals were restored in 2003. In 2005, Fisk voted to sell two Stieglitz Collection paintings—O'Keeffe’s "Radiator Building" and Hartley’s "Painting No. 3," estimated at up to $45 million—challenged by the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum, but the challenge failed. A joint agreement was established with the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, sharing presentation and display rights every two years, with ownership remaining with Fisk. In 2016, during its sesquicentennial, the collection was displayed at the renovated Carl Van Vechten Gallery. Fisk has a strong academic record, having graduated more African Americans who earn PhDs in the natural sciences than any other institution. Since 2004, the Fisk-Vanderbilt bridge program has helped underrepresented groups access PhD programs in STEM, providing a master’s scholarship and mentorship, with 21 students completing PhDs and 56 pursuing graduate study; the program has a success rate far above the national average of about 50%. The Fisk athletic teams are known as the Bulldogs and compete in the National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics (NAIA), primarily in the HBCU Athletic Conference (HBCUAC) since the 2021–22 academic year, having previously been in the Gulf Coast Athletic Conference (GCAC), the Association of Independent Institutions (AII), the Great South Athletic Conference (GSAC), the Southern Collegiate Athletic Conference (SCAC), and the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference (SIAC). Fisk competes in 14 varsity sports: men’s basketball, cross country, golf, soccer, and track and field (indoor and outdoor); women’s basketball, cross country, golf, gymnastics, tennis, track and field (indoor and outdoor), and volleyball. In 2022, Fisk became the first HBCU to officially add a competitive women’s gymnastics team, which will disband after the 2025–2026 season due to financial concerns. Club sports include cheerleading and dance.
